protocol: DHCP (RFC 2131 / RFC 2132) — DHCPDISCOVER + DHCPOFFER over BOOTP/UDP

Sum check: 236-byte BOOTP fixed part + 4-byte cookie + 27 bytes of options + 33 pad = 300. Every declared option length matches the bytes emitted (opt61 l=7 covers 1 htype + 6 addr; opt12 l=6 covers 6 ASCII bytes; opt55 l=4 covers 4 code bytes). Legal-value choices I made rather than copied from a wire trace: xid 0x3903f326, host name "nexa01", param-request-list {1,3,6,42}, flags B=0 (many clients set 0x8000 instead), and pad target 300 (some stacks pad to 342 or not at all — see gap on pad framing). ROUND-TRIP for this packet: the 33 trailing zeros are NOT recoverable from any decoded capture — they are recoverable only if the decoder records the original total length, or if the encoder happens to use the same pad target. Option order is likewise unconstrained by RFC 2131, so re-encoding from a decoded option set is not guaranteed byte-identical.

captures.notes: Sum check: 236 + 4 cookie + 66 bytes of options = 306. No trailing pad: the message already exceeds the 300-byte BOOTP minimum, so this direction has END-with-no-padding while the DISCOVER has END-then-33-pad. That asymmetry alone defeats any grammar that models the option region as a fixed-size padded block — it must be a sentinel-terminated list whose remainder is ignored. Every length octet was checked against the bytes emitted (opt6 l=8 = 2×4; opt15 l=8 = 8 ASCII bytes; all others l=4 or l=1). Deliberate hazards planted: non-empty sname (fixed 64-byte NUL-padded string, 13 significant bytes), a two-element ipv4 list inside one option, and a lease/T1/T2 triple that is the data-driven timer set the state model must consume. Legal-value choices: siaddr 192.168.0.1 (commonly 0.0.0.0), sname "dhcp.nexa.lan", the option set and its ORDER (RFC 2131 imposes no order except END last).

statefulness:
DHCP is almost entirely state model, and it exercises five of the seven gaps §5 already admits to — plus three it does not list.

LEGAL-MESSAGE-PER-STATE. RFC 2131's client FSM is INIT → SELECTING → REQUESTING → BOUND → RENEWING → REBINDING, with a side branch INIT-REBOOT → REBOOTING. DISCOVER is legal only in INIT/SELECTING. OFFER is acceptable only in SELECTING. ACK means different things in REQUESTING (lease granted, go BOUND), RENEWING (lease extended, stay BOUND with new timers), and after an INFORM (config only, NO address, MUST NOT go BOUND). NAK is legal in REQUESTING/RENEWING/REBINDING and always dumps you to INIT. RELEASE is legal only from BOUND/RENEWING/REBINDING. `validIn` covers all of this fine.

THE CONSTRAINT `validIn` CANNOT EXPRESS. One message code, DHCPREQUEST, has four mutually exclusive field contracts selected by state:
  • SELECTING  — MUST carry option 54 (server-id) and option 50 (requested-IP); ciaddr MUST be 0; broadcast.
  • INIT-REBOOT — MUST carry option 50; MUST NOT carry option 54; ciaddr MUST be 0; broadcast.
  • RENEWING   — ciaddr MUST be the leased address; MUST NOT carry option 50 or 54; UNICAST to the server.
  • REBINDING  — as renewing, but broadcast.
`validIn` gates a whole message; there is no per-state "require field / forbid field / change transport". You can work around it with four message templates that `ref` a shared core (my encode document already factors `bootpFixed` that way), so this is expressible-by-duplication rather than blocking — but the constraint itself is unstated and therefore unenforced, and getting it wrong produces a NAK, not a validation error.

MANDATED CHAINING, AND WHY `requires` IS TOO WEAK. REQUEST(selecting) requires a prior OFFER — `requires:["dhcpOffer"]` says that much. But the real obligation is a DATA dependency on a SPECIFIC offer: correlation is `broadcast`, which §4 says yields a LIST, because several servers may answer one DISCOVER. The client picks one and must echo THAT element's option 54 into its REQUEST and THAT element's yiaddr into option 50. Nothing in v0 selects an element of a broadcast result and binds session state from it. This is the single biggest state-model hole for DHCP.

MUTUAL EXCLUSION. `conflicts` is session-scoped and too coarse. The real exclusions are transaction-scoped: after selecting one OFFER you must not REQUEST another in the same xid; DECLINE and REQUEST are alternatives for the same offer; INFORM must never reach BOUND; and once RELEASE is sent the lease is gone for that xid.

NEGOTIATED CAPABILITY — the gap §5 lists, with a concrete instance. The client asks for a lease (option 51 in the REQUEST) and the server may grant LESS; the client asks for options 1,3,6,42 via option 55 and the server may silently omit any of them (my OFFER honours 1, 3, 6 and drops 42 — that omission is invisible, there is no "not supported" marker). The server may also offer a different address than the one requested. v0 has no primitive to diff requested-vs-granted, so the caller cannot be told "you asked for 12 h and got 4 h" or "NTP was not provided".

CONFIRMED VS PRESUMED — and the confirmation is a DIFFERENT PROTOCOL. After ACK the client presumes it owns yiaddr. RFC 2131 §2.2 says it SHOULD ARP-probe the address first and send DECLINE if something answers. So BOUND is presumed until an ARP probe confirms it, and `confirmedBy:{message:…}` can only name a message in this same document. Symmetrically the server presumes the client took the offer; it only learns otherwise from the absence of a REQUEST (offers are reserved then time out).

DATA-DRIVEN TIMERS — three deadlines, one state. The ACK carries T1 (21600 s), T2 (37800 s) and the lease (43200 s) as three separate options, producing three scheduled transitions out of BOUND/RENEWING/REBINDING. A v0 state has ONE `timeoutMs` and ONE `expires`. You cannot express BOUND→RENEWING at T1, RENEWING→REBINDING at T2, REBINDING→INIT at expiry.

DISCOVERED-BY-FAILURE — two flavours, only one of which v0 handles. The `implies` hook is a good fit for the explicit failure: a NAK on a renewal REQUEST means the lease you thought you held is dead — `{"when":"capture.options[53] == 6", "state":"init", "invalidate":["store.leasedIp","store.serverId"]}`. But the more common discovery is SILENCE: no OFFER, or no ACK, and you only learn the server is gone by a timeout. `implies` hangs off `expect` and is keyed on `capture.*`, which does not exist on a timeout edge — so the "no response ⇒ the network moved / the server died ⇒ fall back" inference is unexpressible.

RETRANSMISSION AND SEQUENCE. RFC 2131 §4.1 mandates randomised exponential backoff — roughly 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 s each ±1 s — and every retransmit MUST reuse the SAME xid while `secs` MUST increase to reflect elapsed acquisition time. `loop:{max:n}` plus a `delay` step gives a fixed-interval loop with no jitter, and it is undefined whether `random.u32` re-evaluates on each loop pass — if it does, the xid changes and every retransmit becomes a new transaction that servers will answer separately. So DHCP needs "stable across retries" and "recomputed per attempt" as distinct evaluation scopes, which v0 does not have.

DEDUP. Relays duplicate DISCOVERs; the same server may OFFER twice. There is no dedup window, so a broadcast collect would surface the same offer as two candidates.

NET: the step graph and `validIn`/`requires`/`implies` get DHCP roughly half-modelled. What is missing and load-bearing is (1) select-one-from-a-broadcast-list and bind session state from it, (2) a timer SET per state rather than a single timeout, (3) requested-vs-granted negotiation, (4) per-state field contracts for one message code, (5) `implies` on timeout edges, and (6) jittered backoff with declared stable-vs-per-attempt value scopes.

gaps.what: No sentinel-terminated repetition. The DHCP options region is a run of TLVs of unknown count that ends at the 0xFF END option (or end of datagram), whichever comes first.
gaps.why: At offset 240 the decoder must walk 35 01 01 / 3d 07 … / 0c 06 … / 37 04 … / ff and stop. §3's only repetition primitives are `repeat:<const>` and `each:"<count expression>"`. The count is not merely unknown, it is uncomputable up front: item sizes are only discovered by walking them. And the two directions differ — DISCOVER has 33 bytes after END, OFFER has 0 — so no fixed size works either.
gaps.proposedFix:
Extend tlvList with a terminator and a bound, and add a `remaining()` span function:
{ "tlvList": { "t":"u8", "l":"u8",
               "until": { "type":"0xff" },
               "maxBytes": "remaining()",
               "onTrailing": "ignore" },
  "as":"options" }
On encode `until` emits the terminator after the last item; on decode it stops the walk. `remaining()` joins len(group:X)/len(after:X) as a third span function, resolving to bytes left in the enclosing layer payload.

gaps.what: No length-less (bare) TLV codes. Options 0x00 PAD and 0xFF END are a single type octet with no length and no value; every other option has t+l+v.
gaps.why: Point v0's `{"tlvList":{"t":"u8","l":"u8",…}}` at offset 240 of the DISCOVER and it walks 53, 61, 12, 55 correctly, then reads t=0xff at offset 266 and consumes offset 267 (0x00, a PAD byte) as its LENGTH, then swallows pad bytes as a value. The remaining 32 zeros then decode as ~16 phantom zero-length options. A generic fixed-shape TLV walker cannot parse DHCP options at all — not a tuning issue, a shape mismatch.

gaps.what: Decode mode has no converter pipeline. A decoded field can only carry `as:` — there is no slot for `| ipv4`, `| mac`, `| ascii`.
gaps.why: `{"u32be":null,"as":"yiaddr"}` over c0 a8 00 0a binds Int 3232235530, not "192.168.0.10". `{"value":null,"repeat":6,"as":"chaddr"}` binds raw Bytes, not "00:0b:82:01:fc:42". The `ipv4` and `mac` converters exist in §6 but are unreachable in decode mode, so decode(encode(x)) != x for every address field in both packets — the encoder consumed ipv4 text, the decoder produced an Int. Recovering it in a `compute` step is exactly the per-protocol code path §7 forbids, and it also breaks the symmetry that makes one field list serve both directions.

gaps.what: `repeat` and `skip` cannot take an expression, so a field's width cannot depend on an earlier decoded field.
gaps.why: chaddr at offset 28 is a fixed 16-byte slot of which only `hlen` bytes (read back at offset 2) are the hardware address; the remaining 16-hlen are NUL fill. Decoding it needs `repeat:"capture.hlen"` then `skip:"16 - capture.hlen"`. §3 shows `"repeat":16` and `"skip":2` as constants — only `each` is documented to take an expression (`"capture.byteCount / 2"`). This is the canonical 'decode requires state carried across fields' case, and it is not exotic: htype 6 (IEEE 802) and htype 32 (InfiniBand) use different hlen with the same 16-byte slot.
gaps.proposedFix:
Declare that `repeat` and `skip` accept the same expression form `each` already does, evaluated over captures already bound at that point in the walk:
{ "value":null, "repeat":"capture.hlen", "as":"chaddr", "via":"mac" },
{ "skip": "16 - capture.hlen" }
A forward reference to a not-yet-bound capture becomes a validation error, mirroring the existing cyclic-span rule.

gaps.what: No random-access / at-offset field. RFC 2131 option 52 (Option Overload) redirects the option parse BACKWARD into the `file` (offset 108) and/or `sname` (offset 44) regions.
gaps.why: If the options at 240 contain `34 01 03`, then options continue inside the 128 bytes at 108 and the 64 bytes at 44 — regions the strictly-forward decoder consumed as opaque blobs ~200 bytes earlier. Every v0 field advances a cursor; there is no seek, no absolute offset, no re-parse of an already-bound capture. My OFFER carries a real 13-byte sname, so an overloaded variant of exactly this packet is unparseable.
gaps.proposedFix:
Add a region field that parses a slice at an absolute or captured offset without moving the main cursor:
{ "region": { "at":108, "len":128 },
  "when": "capture.options[52] != null && (capture.options[52] & 1) != 0",
  "fields": [ { "tlvList": { "t":"u8", "l":"u8", "bare":["0x00","0xff"], "until":{"type":"0xff"} } } ],
  "as": "fileOptions" }
On encode `region` back-patches into the reserved span, which the two-pass machinery already supports.

gaps.what: No accumulate-by-key on decode: RFC 3396 splits an option longer than 255 bytes into multiple instances of the same code that MUST be concatenated on receipt.
gaps.why: An option-55 or option-119 payload over 255 bytes arrives as e.g. `37 ff <255 bytes> 37 2a <42 bytes>` and means ONE 297-byte list. A per-field fold produces two separate options; correct decoding needs an accumulator keyed by option code across the whole walk. Encoding needs the inverse chunking, which no converter provides.
gaps.proposedFix:
Flag it on the tlvList and add the encode-side splitter:
{ "tlvList": { …, "concatByType": true } }        // decode: same-code items concatenated in wire order
plus a bytes converter `chunk(n)` producing List<Bytes> so encode can emit `{"each":"inputs.longOpt | chunk(255)", "as":"c", "fields":[{"u8":"code"},{"u8":"len(group:c)"},{"value":"c"}]}`.

gaps.what: No decode-side assertion and no message discriminator. The magic cookie cannot be required, and DISCOVER/OFFER/REQUEST/ACK/NAK cannot be told apart.
gaps.why: At offset 236 the four bytes 63 82 53 63 are what distinguishes DHCP from bare BOOTP; in decode mode the only way past them is `{"skip":4}`, which silently accepts anything. Worse, all five DHCP message types share byte-identical framing and differ ONLY by option 53 — a value buried inside the TLV list, at a position that varies by sender. v0 has no way to select a parse block on a nested captured value, so `expect` cannot distinguish 'the OFFER I want' from 'a NAK'.
gaps.proposedFix:
Two small additions. (a) assertable const in decode:
{ "const":"63 82 53 63", "assert":"required", "onMismatch":"nomatch" }
(b) a post-parse dispatch on any bound capture:
"parse": { "fields":[ …common… ],
           "dispatch": { "on":"capture.options[53]",
                         "cases": { "1":"parse.discover", "2":"parse.offer",
                                    "5":"parse.ack", "6":"parse.nak" },
                         "default":"nomatch" } }

gaps.what: No typed option schema, so an arbitrary option set cannot be supplied by the caller. `tlvList`'s `items` has no declared item shape and inputs have no record type.
gaps.why: Each DHCP option code has its own value type: 53 = u8 enum, 51/58/59 = u32be seconds, 1/3/28/54 = ipv4, 6 = list<ipv4>, 12/15 = ASCII, 55 = raw u8 array, 61 = {u8 htype, mac}. §6's input types stop at `list<T>` — there is no `list<record>` and no per-code type map. My encode document therefore hard-codes each option as an explicit t/l/v triple. That reproduces THESE two captures byte-exactly, but it means the document encodes one fixed option set, not DHCP.
gaps.proposedFix:
Declare an option schema as a const and let tlvList consume it in both directions:
"consts": { "DHCP_OPTIONS": { "1":"ipv4", "3":"ipv4", "6":"list<ipv4>", "12":"ascii",
                             "15":"ascii", "28":"ipv4", "51":"u32be", "53":"u8",
                             "54":"ipv4", "55":"bytes", "58":"u32be", "59":"u32be" } }
{ "tlvList": { "t":"u8", "l":"u8", "schema":"consts.DHCP_OPTIONS",
               "items":"inputs.options", "default":"bytes" } }
with input type `list<{code:u8, value:any}>`. Unknown codes fall back to `bytes`, which keeps forward compatibility with vendor options.

gaps.what: `bits` cannot span a byte boundary, has no declared bit order, and has no decode form.
gaps.why: The BOOTP flags field at offset 10 is 1 bit B (broadcast) + 15 bits MBZ across two bytes. §3's only example sums to exactly 8, so a 1+15 split is at best undefined; whether n counts MSB-first is never stated. And in decode mode there is no `as:` per sub-field, so the B flag cannot be captured at all — my decode falls back to `{"u16be":null,"as":"flags"}`, losing the named bit. This matters semantically: B=1 vs B=0 changes whether the server unicasts the OFFER to an address the client does not yet own.
gaps.proposedFix:
Give `bits` an explicit container and symmetric naming:
{ "bits": { "width":"u16be", "order":"msbFirst",
            "fields":[ { "n":1,  "name":"broadcast", "value":"inputs.bcastFlag", "as":"bcast" },
                       { "n":15, "name":"mbz",       "value":"0" } ] } }
Validate that the sub-field widths sum exactly to the container width. `order` defaults to msbFirst and must be stated in the spec, not inferred.

gaps.what: `expect` correlation cannot combine `broadcast` and `token`, and cannot match on more than one field.
gaps.why: A DHCP client must accept OFFERs from ANY server (so: broadcast, yielding a list — several servers may answer) but must discard any whose xid != the DISCOVER's xid OR whose chaddr != its own MAC. §4 presents socket / token / broadcast as three alternatives, and `token` is described as a single echoed value. There is no way to say 'collect all responders for N ms, keeping only those matching this two-field predicate'.
gaps.proposedFix:
Make correlation a predicate plus a collection policy:
{ "id":"gotOffers", "kind":"expect", "message":"dhcpOffer",
  "correlate": { "kind":"broadcast",
                 "match":"capture.xid == state.xid && capture.chaddr == device.mac",
                 "collectMs": 10000, "minResponders": 1, "dedupBy":"capture.options[54]" },
  "as":"offers" }
`dedupBy` also closes the retransmission-dedup gap §5 lists.

gaps.what: The `udp` layer cannot express a client with no IP address: source 0.0.0.0:68 → 255.255.255.255:67, receiving a reply addressed to an IP it does not yet own.
gaps.why: This is the defining transport property of DHCP — the client is asking for the address it would need in order to have a normal socket. §2 says the udp layer's engine 'sets ports + broadcast flag' with IP/Ethernet done by the OS, and `ip`/`ethernet` are elevation-gated or forbidden. On most OSes an ordinary UDP socket cannot bind 0.0.0.0 as a source with no configured address, and if the client sets flags B=0 (as my DISCOVER does) the server may UNICAST the OFFER to 192.168.0.10 with a hand-poked ARP entry — a datagram the kernel will drop because no interface owns that address. So the encode document is correct and the packet still never arrives.
gaps.proposedFix:
Let the udp layer declare the unbound/raw case explicitly rather than forcing the ethernet escape hatch:
{ "kind":"udp", "srcPort":68, "dstPort":67,
  "srcIp":"0.0.0.0", "dstIp":"255.255.255.255",
  "bind":"unbound", "acceptForeignDst":true, "iface":"adapter.name" }
The engine maps this to AF_PACKET/BPF or an IP_HDRINCL raw socket and gates it on one capability (raw-socket, not full elevation), so the protocol document stays declarative.

gaps.what: State model: `requires` proves a prior message happened but cannot bind data from a SPECIFIC element of a broadcast response list.
gaps.why: REQUEST(selecting) must echo option 54 and yiaddr from the ONE offer the client chose, out of N received. §5 gives `requires:["login"]` (existence) and §4 says broadcast correlation yields a list, but nothing selects an element and promotes its fields into session scope. With two DHCP servers on the segment the document has no way to say which one it is now talking to.
gaps.proposedFix:
Add a `select` step kind that picks from a list result and binds scoped state:
{ "id":"chooseOffer", "kind":"select", "from":"state.offers",
  "pick":"first",            // or "maxBy":"it.options[51]" to prefer the longest lease
  "bind": { "session.serverId":"it.options[54]",
            "session.offeredIp":"it.yiaddr",
            "session.offeredLease":"it.options[51]" } }
Messages then reference session.serverId, and `requires:["chooseOffer"]` carries the data dependency, not just the ordering.

gaps.what: State model: a state has one `timeoutMs` and one `expires`, but DHCP derives THREE deadlines with three different destination states from one response.
gaps.why: The ACK/OFFER carries option 51 (lease, 43200 s), option 58 (T1, 21600 s) and option 59 (T2, 37800 s) — bytes at offsets 251, 257, 263 of my OFFER. They mean BOUND→RENEWING at T1, RENEWING→REBINDING at T2, REBINDING→INIT at lease expiry. `"connected": {"timeoutMs":30000, "onTimeout":"disconnected"}` expresses one of the three.
gaps.proposedFix:
Replace the single timeout with a timer set whose deadlines are expressions:
"bound": { "timers": [
   { "at":"store.t1Utc",           "to":"renewing" },
   { "at":"store.t2Utc",           "to":"rebinding" },
   { "at":"store.leaseExpiresUtc", "to":"init",
     "invalidate":["store.leasedIp","store.serverId"] } ] }
Keep `timeoutMs`/`onTimeout` as sugar for a one-element timer set.

gaps.what: State model: no negotiated-capability primitive — the response may grant LESS than was requested, silently.
gaps.why: The concrete instance: my DISCOVER's option 55 asks for codes 1, 3, 6 and 42 (offset 262..265); the OFFER supplies 1, 3, 6 and simply omits 42 — there is no 'not supported' marker anywhere on the wire, the absence IS the answer. Likewise a client may request a 24 h lease and be granted 12 h (option 51 = 0x0000a8c0). §5 already lists this as a known gap; DHCP confirms it, and shows it has two forms: a downgraded scalar and a silently-dropped set member.
gaps.proposedFix:
Declare the negotiation on the message so the engine can diff and surface it:
"negotiated": [
  { "name":"lease", "requested":"inputs.leaseSecs", "granted":"capture.options[51]",
    "rule":"granted <= requested", "onShortfall":"accept" },
  { "name":"options", "requested":"inputs.prl", "granted":"capture.options | keys",
    "rule":"subset", "onShortfall":"warn", "as":"state.unsatisfied" } ]
The shortfall becomes a first-class capture the caller can read, instead of an invisible omission.

gaps.what: State model: confirmation of a presumed state can require a DIFFERENT protocol. `confirmedBy` can only name a message in this document.
gaps.why: After ACK the client presumes it owns yiaddr (192.168.0.10), but RFC 2131 §2.2 says it SHOULD ARP-probe first and send DHCPDECLINE if anything answers. So BOUND is presumed-only until an ARP exchange confirms it, and ARP is a different protocol document entirely. §5's `"confirmedBy":{"message":"getRelay",…}` assumes intra-document confirmation.
gaps.proposedFix:
Let confirmedBy name a foreign protocol, resolved through the same registry the step graph uses:
"confirmedBy": { "protocol":"arp-v4", "message":"arpProbe",
                 "with": { "target":"capture.yiaddr" },
                 "matches":"capture.replies | len == 0",
                 "onDisproved": { "send":"dhcpDecline", "state":"init" } }

gaps.what: State model: no retransmission policy, and no declared distinction between values that must stay STABLE across retries and values that must be RECOMPUTED per attempt.
gaps.why: RFC 2131 §4.1 mandates randomised exponential backoff (≈4, 8, 16, 32, 64 s, each ±1 s). Within one acquisition every retransmit MUST reuse the same xid (offset 4, 0x3903f326) while `secs` (offset 8) MUST increase to reflect elapsed time. v0 offers `loop:{max:n}` plus a `delay` step — fixed interval, no jitter — and never says whether `random.u32` re-evaluates on each pass. If it does, each retransmit becomes a distinct transaction and every server answers it separately.
gaps.proposedFix:
Declare retry on the send/expect pair with explicit value scoping:
"retry": { "schedule":"exponential", "baseMs":4000, "maxMs":64000,
           "jitterMs":1000, "max":5,
           "stable":["state.xid"],            // evaluated once per transaction
           "perAttempt":["secs"] }            // re-evaluated each send
This also gives `seq.next` and `random.*` a defined evaluation point, which they currently lack.

gaps.what: State model: `implies` hangs off `expect` and is keyed on `capture.*`, so nothing can be inferred from a TIMEOUT.
gaps.why: The commonest DHCP state discovery is silence: no OFFER after the backoff schedule exhausts means there is no server on this segment; no ACK while RENEWING means fall through to REBINDING and broadcast. §5's example `{"when":"capture.status == 401", …}` needs a response to exist. NAK is handled well; silence is not.
gaps.proposedFix:
Allow implies entries on non-capture outcomes:
"implies": [ { "on":"timeout", "after":"retry.exhausted", "state":"init",
               "emitFact":{ "net.dhcp.serverPresent":false, "confidence":"likely", "ttl":"PT5M" } },
             { "on":"match", "when":"capture.options[53] == 6", "state":"init",
               "invalidate":["store.leasedIp","store.serverId"] } ]

gaps.what: `pad` has no declared reference frame and no declared overflow behaviour.
gaps.why: `{"pad":{"to":300,…}}` — 300 bytes measured from where? Message start, enclosing group start, or current layer payload start? My DISCOVER needs message scope (267 emitted → 33 pad bytes → 300). And my OFFER is already 306 bytes: is the same field an error, a no-op, or a truncation? The two captures differ precisely on this, so the ambiguity is load-bearing, not theoretical.

gaps.what: Arithmetic and comparison operators are used in examples but never declared.
gaps.why: §3's decode example uses `capture.byteCount / 2` and §5 uses `capture.status == 200`, yet §6's converter table lists no operators and no precedence. DHCP needs subtraction for `secs` (`now.epochSeconds - state.acqStartUtc`), bitwise AND for option 52 overload flags (`capture.options[52] & 1`), and `&&` for the two-field OFFER correlation predicate. Without a declared grammar the claim that 'type errors are caught at validate time' cannot hold.
gaps.proposedFix: Declare the operator set and precedence in §6 alongside the pipeline: `+ - * / % & | ^ ~ << >> == != < <= > >= && || ! ?:`, with indexing `x[k]` for map/list access (needed for `capture.options[53]`), and give each operator accepted/produced ProtoValue kinds exactly as converters do.

gaps.what: No fixed-width NUL-padded string type: `pad(n,fill,side)` is silent on over-length input, and there is no decode-side inverse.
gaps.why: `sname` is 64 bytes and `file` is 128 bytes, NUL-padded (my OFFER: 13 significant bytes at offset 44 followed by 51 zeros). Encoding a 70-character server name through `ascii | pad(64,'00','right')` has undefined behaviour — DHCP requires truncation, not overflow. Decoding gives back all 64 bytes with no way to strip the fill, so decode(encode("dhcp.nexa.lan")) yields 64 bytes, not the original 13-char string.
gaps.proposedFix:
Split the two intents and add the inverse: declare `pad(n,fill,side)` as error-on-overflow, add `fit(n,fill,side)` that truncates, and add `cstr` (Bytes→Text, stops at the first 0x00) as the decode-side inverse used via `via`:
{ "value":null, "repeat":64, "as":"sname", "via":"cstr" }

gaps.what: Round-trip is not byte-exact in principle: option ORDER and PAD QUANTITY are unconstrained on the wire but unrecoverable from a decoded option set.
gaps.why: RFC 2131 imposes no ordering on options (only END last), so my OFFER's 53,54,51,58,59,1,3,6,15,28 is one legal permutation of ~3.6 million. Decoding into a code→value map loses the order, and re-encoding produces different bytes for the same semantic content. Likewise the DISCOVER's 33 trailing PAD bytes are recoverable only because I happened to choose 300 as the encoder's pad target — a client padding to 342 or not padding at all decodes identically and re-encodes differently. So encode(decode(bytes)) == bytes holds for these two captures by coincidence of matching conventions, not by construction.
gaps.proposedFix:
Make wire order and trailing fill explicit captures so the encoder can replay them:
{ "tlvList": { …, "preserveOrder":true }, "as":"options" }   // decode emits an ordered list, not a map
{ "pad": { "to":"consts.BOOTP_MIN", … }, "as":"padLen" }      // decode records the observed fill length
and define a document-level "canonical": "reencode" | "preserve" flag, so a protocol can honestly declare which of the two round-trip properties in §7 it guarantees. Silently claiming both for an order-free TLV protocol is the wrong answer.
